title: Contracts and context parameters
goal: By the end you can write a contract that gives callers smart casts and in-place lambdas, explain why the compiler trusts it blindly, declare and call functions with context parameters in Kotlin 2.4, and predict their JVM signature.
opening:
At the print shop, jobs travel between desks in envelopes. A clerk who opens an envelope and sees a paper size written inside knows the job has one. The next clerk down the line doesn't know that, and she would have to open the envelope again. Unless the first clerk stamps the outside: "checked, paper size filled in". Then the next clerk trusts the stamp and gets on with the job.

The Kotlin compiler works the same way. It knows what it saw in the function it is reading, and it never opens a function you call, so your own check function, however careful, teaches it nothing. A contract is the stamp on the outside. The easy trap is the other half of the story: nobody checks a stamp. The compiler believes it, true or not.

In the last lesson we wrote a small language and saw context receivers retire. This time we stamp our own envelopes, watch a false stamp fail at run time, and meet context parameters, the values every clerk on a shift carries without being handed them on each job. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `fun requirePaper(paper: String?) { if (paper == null) throw IllegalArgumentException() }`. After `requirePaper(paper)`, where `paper` is a `String?`, you write `paper.uppercase()`. What happens?
options: It compiles: the compiler sees the throw inside `requirePaper`
Compile error: `paper` is still a `String?` to the compiler
It compiles with a warning
It compiles, and throws `NullPointerException` if `paper` is null
warmup.why: The compiler decides smart casts one function at a time. It doesn't look inside `requirePaper` to learn that a normal return means `paper != null`, so `paper` stays nullable and you get `only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'.` The standard library's `require` gets the smart cast because it declares a contract, the subject of the first section.

sections.h: Your own check functions teach the compiler nothing, until they carry a contract

aside.title: Why doesn't the compiler just read the body of the function?
aside.body: Because then a change inside one function could break code far away. Today a function's signature, its parameter and return types, is the promise callers rely on, and the body is free to change. If smart casts followed bodies, deleting the `throw` from `requirePaper` would silently change which callers compile, perhaps in a module built months ago. Often the body isn't there to read anyway: a library arrives as compiled class files, and the compiler reads their signatures, not their code. A contract keeps the promise next to the signature, written down on purpose, where a reviewer can see it.

sections.h: Finding values by type: ambiguity, limits, and where context parameters fit
sections.body:
The compiler finds context arguments by type, so two values of the same type in the same place are a problem. Take a smaller `note` that needs only a logbook, `context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String)`. Put the front desk's logbook and the back room's logbook in one block, `context(front, back) { note("x") }`, and the compiler won't pick one: `multiple potential context arguments for 'logbook: Logbook' in scope.` The docs give the rule: if several compatible values exist at the same scope level, the compiler reports an ambiguity. A nearer scope still wins over an outer one. In `context(front) { context(back) { note("x") } }`, the inner `back` is used, and the line goes to the back room.

That's a reason to give context parameters specific types: a `Shift` class instead of a bare `String`, a `Logbook` interface instead of a `(String) -> Unit` function type. A bare `String` in a context would match any string in scope.

A few things are not allowed. Constructors can't have context parameters: `context parameters on primary constructors are unsupported.` A property can have them only if it has no backing field, the hidden field that stores a property's value, so it must be a computed getter: `property with context parameters cannot be initialized because it has no backing field.` And two parts are still not stable in Kotlin 2.4. One is passing a context argument by name, as in `note(logbook = front, line = "x")`, an Experimental feature behind `-Xexplicit-context-arguments`. Without the flag, 2.4.21 says it "is only available since language version 2.5". The other is a callable reference, `::note`, which fails with `callable reference to 'context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String): Unit' is unsupported because it has context parameters.` Leave both alone for now.

One change in Kotlin 2.3.20 can surprise you if you bring older preview code forward. Overload resolution, the compiler's choice between functions with the same name, used to prefer a function with context parameters over one without. The 2.3.20 notes say that rule no longer applies, so two overloads that differ only by a context may now be ambiguous.

The JVM shape has two more consequences. Java can call these functions, as long as it passes every argument itself. And adding a context parameter to a public function changes its JVM signature exactly as adding any parameter does, so code compiled against the old version fails with `NoSuchMethodError`. Treat it as a change to the function's public API.

So where do context parameters fit? Not for the long-lived helpers an object is built with: a paper catalogue or a printer driver belongs in the constructor, passed once. Context parameters suit values that belong to the current piece of work and are needed by many small functions: the shift, its logbook, the id of the job in hand, a clock that tests can stop. They are visible in every signature, and the compiler checks them, which a hidden global value never does.

That's also the limit of both tools in this lesson. A contract is believed without checks, and a context argument is found by its type, never by its meaning. Keeping either honest is your job.

A check to finish, with the lab's `review`, which needs a `Logbook` and a `Shift`: `with(Logbook { println(it) }) { context(Shift("late")) { JobRequest(40, "a3", "poster.pdf").review(1_000) } }`. Will it compile, and where does each context argument come from? (It compiles. The `Logbook` comes from the implicit receiver of `with`, and the `Shift` from the `context(...)` block. Each type has exactly one candidate.)

compare.title: A job review with a logbook: Java parameters vs Kotlin contracts and context parameters

java.title: Review.java

kotlin.title: Review.kt

compare.note: The Java version compiles because Java doesn't track null, so `job.paper().toUpperCase()` is accepted whether or not the check ran. The Kotlin version compiles only because the contract tells the compiler that `ensure` returns only when its condition holds. Kotlin's `ensure` is inline, so the message lambda costs nothing when the check passes, while Java builds a `Supplier` on every call. The logbook and the shift appear in Java's signature as two extra parameters that every caller passes on. In Kotlin they are context parameters, filled in by the compiler, and they still compile to exactly those two leading parameters, so Java can call the Kotlin `review` as `review(logbook, shift, job, maxCopies)`.

worked.title: Replace a ThreadLocal shift name with a context parameter

steps.say: The app keeps the current shift's name in a `ThreadLocal`, a variable that holds one value per thread, so that deep helpers can write it into the logbook. It works until a helper runs on another thread, or a test forgets to set it, and then the logbook says `[null]`. The compiler can't help, because nothing in any signature says the value is needed.
Make the need part of the signature. The helper declares a context parameter, and so does every function that calls it, up to the place that knows the shift.

Open the context once, where the job comes in: the function that takes jobs at the counter. Forgetting it is now a compile error, `no context argument for 'shift: Shift' found.`, instead of a `[null]` in the logbook.

Check the price: each function in the chain gets one more JVM parameter, and nothing else. There is no `ThreadLocal` to look up, and the value follows the call instead of the thread, so it survives a move to another thread or into a coroutine (a task that can pause and resume, from the coroutines track).

alt.title: Ensure.java

recap: The compiler never reads the body of a function you call, so your own check functions give no smart casts until they declare a contract.
`returns() implies cond` gives callers a smart cast after a normal return. `callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE)` lets them assign a `val` inside the lambda.
Contracts are Experimental in Kotlin 2.4 and need `@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)`. The compiler trusts them without checking; a false one becomes a `ClassCastException` at run time.

Context parameters, `context(shift: Shift) fun ...`, replaced context receivers: a preview in Kotlin 2.2.0, Stable since 2.4.0. The compiler fills them by type from enclosing context parameters, `context(...) { }` blocks and implicit receivers.
On the JVM they are leading parameters (context, then receiver, then the rest), so Java passes them by hand, and adding one breaks callers that were already compiled.
The limit: a contract is believed, never checked, and a context argument is found by type, never by meaning. Explicit context arguments and callable references are not stable yet.
closing:
We started with envelopes moving between desks. A contract is the stamp on the outside, `returns() implies` or `callsInPlace`, and the compiler believes it without opening the envelope, so a false stamp turns into a `ClassCastException` later. Context parameters are what every clerk carries for the whole shift: passed by the compiler, and on the JVM as plain leading parameters.

In your own code, look for a check function followed by `!!` on the next line. Each one is a missing contract, or a hint that the check should return the value instead.

Next, we'll let the compiler change our classes as they pass through it. What do compiler plugins write into a class file that your source never mentions?

options: A compile error: the body doesn't match the contract
A compiler warning about an unsound contract
It compiles; for a `Reprinted` event the smart cast fails at run time with `ClassCastException`
It compiles, and the smart cast is skipped when the contract is wrong
quiz.why: The compiler trusts `returns ... implies` without checking it, so `event.pages` compiles as if `event` were a `Printed`. At run time the JVM checks the cast it was given, and a `Reprinted` is not a `Printed`. K2 warns only about some `callsInPlace` mistakes, never about `implies`.

quiz.q:
Which contract makes this compile?

```kotlin
val total: Int
withTrayLock { total = tray.count() }
println(total)
```
options: `callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE)` in `withTrayLock`
`callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE)`
No contract: making `withTrayLock` inline is enough
`returns() implies (block != null)`
quiz.why: A `val` must be assigned exactly once, and only `EXACTLY_ONCE` tells the compiler the assignment happens once, during the call. `AT_MOST_ONCE` allows zero runs, so `total` might stay unassigned. Inline alone says nothing about how many times the body calls `block`: without the contract you get `'val' cannot be reassigned.`

quiz.q: How does Java call `context(logbook: Logbook) fun note(line: String)`?
options: `note(line)`, and the logbook comes from a ThreadLocal
`note(logbook, line)`: the context parameter is the first JVM parameter
`note(line, logbook)`
It can't: context parameters are Kotlin-only
quiz.why: On the JVM, context parameters become ordinary parameters placed first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. Java has no context, so it passes the value itself.

quiz.q: Inside `context(front, back) { note("x") }`, both values are `Logbook`s. What does the compiler do?
options: Uses `front`, the first one listed
Uses `back`, the last one listed
Passes both and lets `note` choose
Reports `multiple potential context arguments for 'logbook: Logbook' in scope.`
quiz.why: Context arguments are found by type. Two compatible values at the same scope level are an ambiguity, and the compiler refuses to guess. Give the two roles different types, or open the contexts in nested blocks so that one is nearer.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: a test class was compiled against the stub of the public inline function `ensure`. You fix `ensure` and recompile only `src/main`. What does the old test class run when it calls `ensure`?
options: Your new body, because it's on the classpath
The stub's body, copied into the test class when the test was compiled
Nothing: it fails with `NoSuchMethodError`
Whichever version the class loader finds first
quiz.why: An inline body is pasted into the caller at the caller's compile time, so the old test class holds its own copy of the stub. That's why the lab's tests call `Callers.ensuring`, an ordinary function compiled together with your code.

flashcards.back: A `contract { }` block, the first statement of a function, that tells the compiler something it can't infer: how a lambda is called, or what a normal return implies.

flashcards.front: What does `returns() implies (x != null)` give the caller?
flashcards.back: A smart cast: after the call returns normally, the compiler treats `x` as non-null.

flashcards.front: What does `callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE)` allow in the caller?
flashcards.back: Assigning a `val` inside the lambda, because the compiler now knows the block runs exactly once during the call.

flashcards.front: Does the compiler check a contract against the function body?
flashcards.back: No. It trusts it. A false `returns(true) implies (this is Printed)` compiles and fails at run time with `ClassCastException`.

flashcards.front: What opt-in do contracts need in Kotlin 2.4?
flashcards.back: `@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)`. They are still Experimental. No compiler flag is needed.

flashcards.front: Where can a context argument come from?
flashcards.back: From the caller's surroundings, matched by type: an enclosing function's context parameter, a `context(a, b) { }` block, or an implicit receiver such as `with(x) { }`.

flashcards.front: JVM signature of `context(logbook: Logbook, shift: Shift) fun Job.check(printer: String): Boolean`?
flashcards.back: `static boolean check(Logbook, Shift, Job, String)`: context parameters, then the receiver, then the value parameters.

terms.plain: The compiler treating a variable as a narrower type after a check proves it, such as `String?` to `String` after `!= null`.
A `contract { }` block that states a fact about a function's behavior for callers to rely on. The compiler trusts it.
A contract effect: the lambda runs during the call (it is not kept for later), a given number of times.
A contract effect: if the function returns (or returns a given value), a condition holds.
A parameter declared in `context(...)` that callers don't write; the compiler fills it by type from the surroundings.
The value the compiler finds and passes for a context parameter at a call site.
`@OptIn(...)`: your written agreement to use an Experimental API that may still change.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why `ensure(paper != null, "PAPER_MISSING") { ... }` followed by `paper.uppercase()` compiles only with a contract, and what the compiler does and doesn't check about that contract.
explain_back.answer: The compiler decides smart casts inside one function at a time. It doesn't read the body of `ensure` when it compiles the caller, so without help it has no idea that `ensure` only returns when the condition is true, and `paper` stays a `String?`. The contract `returns() implies condition`, written as the first statement of `ensure`, is a promise stored in the Kotlin metadata: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. When the caller is compiled, the compiler reads that promise and treats `paper` as non-null after the call. It doesn't check the promise. If the body of `ensure` returned without checking, the code would still compile and fail later at run time. The compiler checks only the form: the opt-in is there, the block is the first statement, and for `callsInPlace` it warns about some obvious misuse such as calling the lambda twice or keeping it. So the body should be as simple as the promise, here a single `if (!condition) throw`.

deeper.body:
Kotlin 2.4.0 added one more Experimental contract effect, `returnsResultOf()`, to help the new checker for unused return values. It needs the flag `-Xallow-returns-result-of`, and the release notes warn that using it "produces pre-release binaries that earlier Kotlin compiler versions can't read". Keep it out of libraries that other people use.

The extended contracts from Kotlin 2.2.20 behave in an interesting way on the 2.4.21 compiler. Their old flags (`-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions` and friends) now print `the argument '...' is redundant for the current language version 2.4.`, and a generic `returns(true) implies (this is Ok<T>)` or a `holdsIn` contract compiles without any flag. So they appear to be switched on by default from language version 2.3. They still need their opt-ins, though: `returnsNotNull()` without `@OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class)` is an opt-in error.

If you're moving code from context receivers, three differences bite. Context parameters must be named (or `_`), and a context parameter is not a receiver in the body, so `write("x")` becomes `logbook.write("x")`. `this@Logbook` is gone; use the name or `contextOf<Logbook>()`. And classes can't declare a context any more, only functions and properties.

Finally, a design note. The docs list "simplified dependency injection" as one use, dependency injection being a framework that builds your objects and hands each one the helpers it needs. Treat that with care. A context parameter is resolved when the code is compiled, at each call site, from what is in scope there. A dependency injection framework wires objects when the program starts, from the whole application. They answer different questions: context parameters suit values that belong to one piece of work, and constructors suit helpers that live as long as the object.
